en.title: Information Technology: the whole course
en.short: What an Information Technology course covers, how it is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Information technology (IT) is the use of computers, networks, data and software to solve practical problems in organisations and society. It is wider than programming. It includes choosing hardware, installing and managing operating systems, designing databases, connecting networks, protecting systems, supporting users and improving business processes. A useful way to see the difference is this: computer science asks how computation works and what can be computed; IT asks how to deploy and manage computing safely and usefully for people. The subject also covers the human side, such as usability, ethics, law and service management. It is not only repairing computers, although support work is part of it.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text: Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a BSc in Information Technology commonly runs for four years. The National Universities Commission (NUC) sets minimum academic standards. The older Benchmark Minimum Academic Standards (BMAS) are being replaced by the Core Curriculum and Minimum Academic Standards (CCMAS), so ask which set applies to your intake. Many programmes include industrial training under SIWES; the duration and timing vary, so confirm with your department. Polytechnics award the National Diploma (ND) and Higher National Diploma (HND) under the National Board for Technical Education (NBTE), with a practical focus. In Ghana and Kenya, first degrees often take four years. In England, a degree usually takes three years. In South Africa, a three-year BSc may be followed by an Honours year. A master’s degree usually adds one or two years of advanced courses and a dissertation. Always follow your current departmental regulations.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage builds foundations. You study what IT is, basic mathematics for computing, data representation and digital logic, computer hardware and architecture, operating systems and file management, and programming fundamentals. You also meet application software and spreadsheets, data communications and networking basics, internet and web fundamentals, and information systems in organisations. These courses give you the vocabulary and basic skills for later work.

The core stage deepens the same themes. Intermediate programming and scripting follows first programming. Database design, normalisation and SQL lead on to database administration. Web development builds on programming, networks and databases. Systems analysis and design teaches you to plan systems with users. Data communications and networks leads to network administration. Information security and risk management, cloud computing and virtualisation, data analytics and business intelligence, human-computer interaction, and mobile application development add specialist skills. IT project management, IT service management, enterprise systems and e-business, and professional practice, ethics and law connect technical work to organisations and society.

At master’s level, common courses include advanced data management and big data, cybersecurity governance and digital forensics, cloud-native architecture and edge computing, and research methods in information technology. The exact order varies by institution.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text: Practise on a computer every week. Type the examples, change them and predict what will happen before you run them. For hardware, learn the parts of a computer and how data moves between them. For networks, draw diagrams and use simple commands to inspect addresses and routes. For databases, write SQL queries by hand and test them on a small database. Build small complete systems, such as a stock system for a campus shop or an appointment system for a clinic. They join databases, networks and interfaces, and give you work to show. Keep notes in your own words. Use version control for code. Read official documentation. If you use AI tools, follow your institution’s rules and make sure you can explain every line you submit.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often make these mistakes:
Treating IT as only computer repair or only programming.
Memorising definitions without doing practical work.
Ignoring mathematics and logic because they seem unrelated to IT.
Learning SQL or networking only from notes, without running queries or drawing topologies.
Confusing similar terms, such as authentication and authorisation, backup and archive, or virtualisation and cloud computing.
Leaving security and ethics until the final year, when they should shape every project.
Starting the final project late and leaving no time for testing and writing.
Assuming cloud services are automatically secure or cheap.
Not checking the current rules, standards and deadlines in their own department.

keyPoints: Information technology applies computing to practical problems; it is wider than programming and computer repair.
Degrees differ by country and institution, so check your handbook for length, awards and industrial training.
Study in teaching order: foundations, then core systems and management, then specialist or master’s courses.
Practise weekly on real tools: code, SQL queries, network diagrams and small complete systems.
Learn the vocabulary precisely; many marks are lost by confusing terms such as authentication and authorisation.
Check current standards, security rules and deadlines rather than relying on old notes.

en.title: Foundations of information technology
en.short: Data, information, knowledge and systems, IT system parts, IT versus computer science, careers and digital literacy.

sections.heading: Data to knowledge
sections.text:
Data are raw facts and symbols with no meaning on their own. Information is data that has been processed and given context so that it means something. Knowledge is information combined with experience and judgement, so a person can decide and act. A system is a set of parts working together for a purpose, with inputs, processes, outputs and feedback.

Example: at a clinic in Kano, the reading 38.5 is data. With Amina’s name and the time it becomes information: "Amina’s temperature was 38.5 °C at 09:00." A nurse who knows this is a fever and follows the clinic’s protocol turns it into knowledge.

sections.heading: Parts of an IT system
sections.text:
An IT system has six common parts. Hardware is the physical equipment: computers, phones, printers, cables. Software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do. Data is the raw material the system stores and processes. Networks connect devices so they can share data and services. People are the users, operators and managers. Procedures are the written rules and steps for using the system.

People and procedures are often the weakest parts. A hospital can buy good software but still lose records if staff are not trained or the backup procedure is ignored.

sections.heading: IT and computer science
sections.text:
Information technology is the use of computers and networks to store, process, send and manage information for people and organisations. It focuses on applying, supporting and managing systems.

Computer science studies computation itself: algorithms, data structures, programming languages, and the principles of hardware and software. IT borrows from computer science, but its centre is the working system and its users.

sections.heading: Careers and digital literacy
sections.text:
IT careers include help desk and support, network and systems administration, systems analysis, cybersecurity, database administration and IT project management.

Digital literacy is the ability to use digital tools confidently and critically: to find, evaluate and communicate information, to protect your privacy and data, and to recognise when a tool is the wrong one for the task.

keyPoints: Data are raw facts; information is processed data with context; knowledge adds experience and judgement.
An IT system combines hardware, software, data, networks, people and procedures.
IT applies and manages computing systems for organisations; computer science studies computation and its principles.
People and procedures are as important as hardware and software in a working system.
Digital literacy means using digital tools safely, critically and effectively.
IT careers include support, administration, analysis, security and project management.

en.title: Mathematics for information technology
en.short: Number bases, algebra, sets, logic, graphs, percentages, statistics and probability for IT.

sections.heading: Number bases
sections.text:
A base b numeral uses digits 0 to b−1, and place values are powers of b. Binary is base 2, hexadecimal base 16. To convert 1011₂ to decimal: 1×8 + 0×4 + 1×2 + 1×1 = 11. To convert 11 to hexadecimal: 11 = B.

Add binary by carrying when a column reaches 2: 1011₂ + 0110₂ = 10001₂ (11 + 6 = 17). In hexadecimal, A=10, B=11, ... F=15. Check: 0xB + 0x6 = 0x11 (11 + 6 = 17).

sections.heading: Algebra and functions
sections.text:
Algebra uses letters for unknown numbers. Solve 3x + 5 = 20: subtract 5, then divide by 3, so x = 5. A function maps each input to one output. For f(x)=2x+1, f(3)=7.

On a graph, x is horizontal and y vertical; a straight line y=mx+c has gradient m and intercept c. The gradient is change in y ÷ change in x.

sections.heading: Sets and logic
sections.text:
A set is a collection of distinct objects. A ∪ B contains elements in A or B; A ∩ B contains elements in both. If A={1,2,3} and B={3,4}, then A ∪ B={1,2,3,4} and A ∩ B={3}.

Logic uses propositions that are true or false. NOT reverses truth; AND is true only when both parts are true; OR is true when at least one is true. A truth table lists all cases.

sections.heading: Percentages and statistics
sections.text:
A percentage is a fraction of 100. To find 15% of 240, calculate 0.15 × 240 = 36. A percentage increase from 200 to 250 is (250−200) ÷ 200 × 100 = 25%.

Descriptive statistics summarise data: mean = sum ÷ count, median is the middle value, mode is most frequent. For 2,4,4,10: mean = 20 ÷ 4 = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Probability is a number from 0 to 1. For equally likely outcomes, P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. A fair die gives P(4)=1/6.

keyPoints: To convert a base b numeral, multiply each digit by its place value b^n and add.
Binary addition carries at 2; hexadecimal digits A to F stand for 10 to 15.
Solve linear equations by doing the same operation to both sides; for y = mx + c, m is the gradient.
A ∪ B is the union, A ∩ B is the intersection; AND is true only when both propositions are true.
Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100; mean = sum ÷ count.
Probability of an equally likely event = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.

en.title: Data representation and digital logic
en.short: Bits, bytes, binary integers, text, image and sound encoding, and Boolean logic with gates.

sections.heading: Bits and bytes
sections.text:
A bit is one binary digit, 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits, so it has 2⁸ = 256 patterns. Binary is positional base 2: each place is worth twice the one to its right.

Example: 1011 0110 = 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182. In fours, 1011 = B and 0110 = 6, so the byte is B6 in hexadecimal.

sections.heading: Integers and text
sections.text:
Unsigned binary holds zero and positive values only. Two’s complement holds negatives: in 8 bits the leftmost bit has weight −128, so the range is −128 to +127. To negate, flip every bit and add 1. Example: 6 is 0000 0110; flipped, 1111 1001; plus 1 gives 1111 1010, which is −6.

Text uses a code per character. ASCII defines 128 codes in 7 bits. Unicode assigns a code point to characters across the world’s scripts, and UTF-8 stores them in one to four bytes, its first 128 matching ASCII.

sections.heading: Images and sound
sections.text:
Raster images are a grid of pixels, each storing a colour. Colour depth is the bits per pixel; 24 bits give 2²⁴ colours. Size in bytes = width × height × colour depth ÷ 8. Example: 800 × 600 at 24 bits = 11,520,000 bits = 1,440,000 bytes.

Sound is sampled: sample rate is samples per second, bit depth is bits per sample. Size = rate × depth × channels × seconds ÷ 8. Example: 44,100 Hz, 16 bits, stereo, 10 s = 14,112,000 bits = 1,764,000 bytes.

sections.heading: Boolean logic and gates
sections.text:
Boolean logic uses two values, 0 and 1. NOT inverts. AND is 1 only when both inputs are 1. OR is 1 when at least one is. XOR is 1 when the inputs differ; NAND is AND followed by NOT.

A truth table lists every input combination with its output. Two inputs give four rows: AND gives 0, 0, 0, 1 and OR gives 0, 1, 1, 1. Gates are circuits that compute these functions.

keyPoints: A byte is 8 bits and gives 256 patterns; binary is positional base 2.
In 8-bit two’s complement the range is −128 to +127; negate by flipping bits and adding 1.
ASCII has 128 codes; Unicode covers other scripts and UTF-8 stores it in one to four bytes.
Image size in bytes = width × height × colour depth ÷ 8.
Sound size in bytes = sample rate × bit depth × channels × seconds ÷ 8.
AND, OR, NOT, XOR and NAND are defined by truth tables, and gates compute them.

en.title: Computer hardware and architecture
en.short: CPU, memory, storage, input and output, motherboard buses, performance and basic troubleshooting.

sections.heading: Processor and memory
sections.text:
The central processing unit (CPU) runs instructions. It has a control unit, an arithmetic logic unit (ALU) and registers. The control unit fetches and decodes instructions; the ALU does arithmetic and logic. Registers are tiny fast storage inside the CPU.

Memory is working storage. Random access memory (RAM) is volatile: it loses data when power goes off. Read only memory (ROM) keeps firmware. Cache is small fast memory near the CPU that reduces the wait for RAM. The von Neumann architecture stores program and data in the same memory.

sections.heading: Storage and input/output
sections.text:
Storage keeps data when power is off. A hard disk drive (HDD) uses spinning magnetic platters; a solid state drive (SSD) uses flash memory and has no moving parts. Storage is slower than RAM but larger and cheaper per byte.

Input devices bring data in, such as a keyboard, mouse or scanner. Output devices send results out, such as a monitor, printer or speaker. Some devices do both, such as a touchscreen.

sections.heading: Motherboard and buses
sections.text:
The motherboard is the main circuit board. It connects the CPU, memory, storage and input/output devices. A bus is a shared path for data, addresses and control signals. The system bus links the CPU to memory; input/output buses link to peripherals.

A port is a connection point, such as USB. An expansion slot lets you add a card. The chipset manages communication between components.

sections.heading: Performance and troubleshooting
sections.text:
Performance depends on clock speed, instructions per program, cycles per instruction (CPI) and memory speed. CPU time = instruction count × CPI × clock cycle time. Clock cycle time = 1 ÷ clock rate.

Example: 2 × 10⁹ instructions, CPI 1.5, clock rate 3 × 10⁹ Hz.
Cycle time = 1 ÷ (3 × 10⁹) s.
CPU time = 2 × 10⁹ × 1.5 ÷ (3 × 10⁹) = 1.0 s.

For basic troubleshooting, check power and cables first, then listen for beeps, reseat memory and cards, and test one change at a time. Back up data before repairs.

keyPoints: CPU time = instruction count × CPI × clock cycle time.
Clock cycle time = 1 ÷ clock rate.
RAM is volatile; ROM keeps firmware and storage keeps data without power.
A bus carries data, addresses and control signals between components.
Check power, cables and connections first when troubleshooting hardware.
Back up data before opening or repairing a computer.

en.title: Operating systems and file management
en.short: OS functions, interfaces, file systems, accounts, permissions, installation, command line, backups and maintenance.

sections.heading: Operating system functions
sections.text:
An operating system (OS) is system software that manages hardware and provides services to programs. It schedules processes, allocates memory, loads device drivers, stores files and enforces access rules.

It also provides the user interface. A graphical user interface (GUI) uses windows, icons, menus and a pointer. A command line interface (CLI) accepts typed commands. The GUI is easier to learn; the CLI is faster for repeated tasks.

sections.heading: Files and paths
sections.text:
A file system is the method an OS uses to name, store, find and protect files and folders. It keeps metadata such as size and permissions. Common examples are NTFS on Windows, ext4 on Linux and APFS on macOS.

A path names a file’s location. An absolute path starts at the root, such as C:\Users\Amina\report.docx or /home/amina/report.txt. A relative path starts from the current folder. Extensions help programs but do not prove content.

sections.heading: Accounts and permissions
sections.text:
An account identifies a user. It authenticates the user and applies permissions. A standard account runs ordinary programs; an administrator can install software and change settings. Use a standard account for daily work.

Permissions state who may read, write or execute a file. Unix and Linux use owner, group and others, each with read, write and execute bits. Windows uses access control lists (ACLs). Example: chmod 640 gives owner read and write (6 = 4 + 2), group read (4), others none (0).

sections.heading: Installation and upkeep
sections.text:
Installation usually means partitioning a disk, formatting partitions, copying the OS, installing a bootloader and drivers. The command line uses short commands: ls or dir lists files, cd changes folder, mkdir makes a folder, cp or copy copies, rm or del deletes.

Back up important files to a separate medium and test a restore. A common guideline is three copies, on two media, with one off-site. Maintenance includes updates, removing unused software and monitoring free space. Defragment hard disks, not solid-state drives. Case: Amina in Kano backs up weekly to an external drive and cloud storage.

keyPoints: An operating system manages hardware, schedules processes, allocates memory, stores files and enforces access rules.
A GUI uses windows, icons, menus and a pointer; a CLI accepts typed commands and can be scripted.
Common file systems are NTFS on Windows, ext4 on Linux and APFS on macOS.
Permissions control who may read, write or execute a file; Unix uses owner, group and others, while Windows uses ACLs.
Installation sets up partitions, a file system, a bootloader and drivers, so back up first.
Back up important files to a separate medium and test a restore; maintain the system with updates and free-space checks.

en.title: Programming fundamentals
en.short: Variables, data types, control flow, functions, arrays, input and output, debugging and small programs.

sections.heading: Variables and types
sections.text:
A variable is a named storage location whose value can change while a program runs. A data type says what kind of value it holds: integer (whole number), real (decimal), character, string (text) or Boolean (true or false).

Declare a variable before use. Assignment stores a value: age = 19. Some languages need a type declaration, such as int age = 19; others infer it. Integer division can lose information: 7 ÷ 2 gives 3, not 3.5.

sections.heading: Control flow and functions
sections.text:
Control flow decides which statements run and how often. A conditional runs a block only when a condition is true: if score ≥ 50 then print pass else print fail. A loop repeats a block: while count < 5 do ... . Conditions use comparison operators (=, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥) and logical operators (and, or, not). Check loop boundaries.

A function is a named block that takes inputs (parameters), does one job and returns a result. Functions avoid repetition and make testing easier.

sections.heading: Arrays and input/output
sections.text:
An array stores several values of the same type under one name, accessed by an index. In most languages the first index is 0, so scores[0] is the first item and scores[3] is the fourth. Check bounds: reading scores[4] from a four-item array is an error.

Input brings data into a program, often from the keyboard or a file. Output sends results to the screen or a file. Validate input: reject text when a number is expected and handle zero before dividing.

sections.heading: Debugging and a small program
sections.text:
Debugging means finding and fixing errors. Syntax errors break the language rules and stop the program. Logic errors let it run but give wrong results. Read error messages, trace values with print statements or a debugger, and test boundary values.

Small program: read a, b, c; total = a + b + c; average = total ÷ 3; print average.
With a = 6, b = 8, c = 10: total = 24 and average = 8. Test zero and negative values too.

keyPoints: A variable is a named storage location, and its data type controls what values and operations it allows.
Control flow uses conditionals and loops to choose which statements run and how often.
A function takes parameters, performs one job and returns a result, which reduces repetition.
Arrays store several values under one name and are indexed from 0 in most languages.
Validate input and check array bounds before using data.
Debug by reading error messages, tracing values and testing boundary cases.

en.title: Application software and spreadsheets
en.short: Word processing, presentations, spreadsheet formulas, functions, charts, sorting, filtering and file formats.

sections.heading: Documents and slides
sections.text: Application software is written for end-user tasks rather than for running the computer itself. A word processor creates and edits formatted text: headings, tables, images and page layout. A presentation program arranges slides for a talk; each slide holds text, images and sometimes charts. Use styles and slide masters to keep formatting consistent, and check spelling and accessibility before sharing.

sections.heading: Spreadsheet formulas
sections.text: A spreadsheet is a grid of cells, each named by column letter and row number, such as B3. A formula starts with = and calculates from cell references. Relative references change when copied; absolute references such as $B$3 stay fixed. Example: quantities in A2:A4 are 2, 3, 5 and unit prices in B2:B4 are 150, 200, 100. C2 = A2*B2 gives 300, C3 gives 600 and C4 gives 500. =SUM(C2:C4) gives 1,400. Check: 300 + 600 + 500 = 1,400.

sections.heading: Functions and charts
sections.text: Functions are built-in formulas with names, such as SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and IF. They save time and reduce typing errors. A chart turns numbers into a picture. Choose the type to match the message: a column chart compares categories, a line chart shows change over time, and a pie chart shows parts of one whole. Label axes and units, and do not use a pie chart for many categories.

sections.heading: Sorting, filtering and formats
sections.text: Sorting reorders rows by one or more keys, such as price from low to high. Filtering hides rows that fail a condition, such as sales above 500, without deleting them. Collaboration lets several people edit a shared file, add comments and see version history; agree who owns each part to avoid conflicts. Common formats include .docx, .pptx and .xlsx for Microsoft Office, .odt, .odp and .ods for OpenDocument, .pdf for fixed layout, and .csv for plain tabular data. CSV keeps values but not formulas, charts or formatting.

keyPoints: Application software supports end-user tasks such as word processing, presentations and spreadsheets.
A formula begins with = and uses cell references; relative references change when copied, while absolute references such as $B$3 stay fixed.
In the example, =A2*B2 gives 300 and =SUM(C2:C4) gives 1,400.
Functions are named built-in calculations such as SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and IF.
Charts should match the data: column for categories, line for time, pie for parts of one whole.
Sorting reorders rows, filtering hides rows, and collaboration uses shared editing, comments and version history; common formats include .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, .odt, .odp, .ods, .pdf and .csv.

en.title: Data communications and networking basics
en.short: Signals, media, LANs and WANs, topologies, OSI and TCP/IP models, IP addressing and network devices.

sections.heading: Signals and media
sections.text:
Data communications moves data between devices using agreed rules called protocols. A signal is a changing physical quantity, such as voltage, light or a radio wave, that carries data. Analogue signals vary continuously; digital signals use a small set of levels, usually two.

Transmission media are guided or unguided. Guided media confine the signal: twisted-pair copper, coaxial cable and fibre optic cable. Unguided media travel through air or space: radio, microwave and infrared. Fibre gives high data capacity and immunity to electrical interference; copper is cheaper. All media suffer attenuation, so the signal weakens with distance.

sections.heading: LANs, WANs, topologies
sections.text:
A local area network (LAN) covers a limited area, such as a building, and is usually owned by one organisation. A wide area network (WAN) links sites over a large area, often through a telecommunications provider.

A topology is the arrangement of links and devices. In a star, devices connect to a central switch; this is common in Ethernet LANs. A bus shares one backbone, a ring passes data around a loop, and a mesh uses many paths for resilience. Physical topology describes cables; logical topology describes data flow.

sections.heading: Models and addressing
sections.text:
The OSI model is a seven-layer reference model: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. The TCP/IP model has four layers: network access, internet, transport and application. OSI helps describe duties; TCP/IP names protocols used in practice.

An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers. A subnet mask marks network and host bits. Example: 192.168.10.37 with mask 255.255.255.0. The network is 192.168.10.0, the host part is 37, and the broadcast address is 192.168.10.255. The block has 2⁸ = 256 addresses; 254 are usable.

sections.heading: Network devices
sections.text: Common devices: a hub repeats signals to all ports; a switch forwards frames (data-link units) by MAC address (a hardware address) inside a LAN; a router forwards IP packets between networks; a wireless access point connects Wi-Fi clients; a modem converts signals for a provider line.

keyPoints: Data communications uses protocols, and signals carry data over guided or unguided media that all suffer attenuation.
LANs cover limited areas; WANs link distant sites, often through a provider.
Star, bus, ring and mesh describe topologies; star is common in Ethernet LANs.
OSI has seven layers; TCP/IP has four and matches practical protocols.
For an IPv4 block with prefix /n, addresses = 2^(32 − n) and usable hosts = 2^(32 − n) − 2.
Switches forward frames by MAC address, routers forward IP packets between networks, and hubs repeat signals to all ports.

en.title: Internet and web fundamentals
en.short: How the internet and web work: architecture, HTTP, URLs, browsers, search, email, cloud and safe use.

sections.heading: Internet architecture
sections.text: The internet is a network of networks. It moves data between devices using agreed protocols: IP for addressing and routing, and TCP or UDP for transport. Internet service providers (ISPs) connect homes and organisations to regional and global backbone links, and routers forward packets hop by hop. The Domain Name System (DNS) maps names to IP addresses. No single owner controls it; open standards come from bodies such as the IETF and W3C.

sections.heading: Web, HTTP and URLs
sections.text: The World Wide Web is a service on the internet: linked resources identified by URLs and fetched mainly with HTTP. A URL has a scheme (https), host (example.org), optional port, path, query and fragment. HTTP is a request-response protocol. GET requests a resource; POST sends data. Status codes such as 200 OK and 404 Not Found report the result. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, so traffic is encrypted and the server is authenticated. Browsers fetch HTML, CSS and JavaScript and render pages. Search engines crawl pages, build an index and rank results.

sections.heading: Email and cloud
sections.text: Email uses SMTP to send messages between mail servers. Clients retrieve mail with IMAP, which keeps folders on the server, or POP3, which usually downloads it. Cloud services deliver computing over the internet: IaaS gives virtual machines and storage, PaaS gives a platform for code, and SaaS gives ready applications such as webmail. Under the shared responsibility model the provider secures the physical infrastructure, while the user secures accounts, data and access settings.

sections.heading: Safe online behaviour
sections.text: Treat unsolicited links and attachments as suspect. Phishing messages imitate trusted organisations to steal passwords or money. Use long unique passphrases, enable multi-factor authentication, update software, and check for HTTPS before entering personal data. Back up important files. Case: Amina gets an email saying her bank account will close unless she logs in through a link. The address is not her bank’s domain. She does not click; she opens the bank site herself and calls the number on her card.

keyPoints: The internet is a network of networks: IP addresses and routes data, TCP or UDP transports it, and DNS maps names to IP addresses.
The web is a service on the internet; URLs identify resources and HTTP is the request-response protocol that transfers them.
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, which encrypts traffic and authenticates the server.
Browsers render HTML, CSS and JavaScript; search engines crawl, index and rank pages.
Email uses SMTP to send and IMAP or POP3 to retrieve; cloud services offer IaaS, PaaS and SaaS under a shared responsibility model.
Safe online behaviour includes unique passphrases, multi-factor authentication, updates, backups and suspicion of unsolicited links.

en.title: Information systems in organisations
en.short: How transaction, management, decision support and executive systems, ERP and e-commerce serve organisations.

sections.heading: Four system types
sections.text:
An information system collects, processes, stores and distributes data to support work and decisions. A transaction processing system (TPS) records routine events such as sales and payments. It must be fast and reliable.

A management information system (MIS) summarises TPS data into regular reports, such as weekly sales by branch, for managers monitoring performance. A decision support system (DSS) helps with less routine choices. It combines data with models, for example a cash-flow forecast under different price assumptions, and lets the user ask what if. An executive information system (EIS) gives senior managers a concise view of key indicators, with trends and drill-down, meaning you can move from a summary to the detail behind it. The types overlap; labels describe purpose and decision level.

sections.heading: Processes and ERP
sections.text:
A business process is a set of linked activities that produces a result, such as order to delivery. Information systems support processes by passing data between steps, reducing delays and errors.

Enterprise resource planning (ERP) is integrated software with shared modules for finance, purchasing, inventory, production and human resources. One database means a sale can update stock and accounts together. ERP projects are costly and need process redesign, so they can fail if the organisation is not ready. A distributor might use one system so an order checks stock, raises an invoice and updates the ledger.

sections.heading: E-commerce
sections.text:
E-commerce is buying and selling goods or services over electronic networks. Business-to-business (B2B) trade is between firms; business-to-consumer (B2C) is to individual consumers.

Online catalogues, payment systems and order tracking are information systems. They lower some search and paperwork costs but create needs for security, delivery and returns handling. E-commerce data also feeds MIS and DSS.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text:
Suppose Amina runs a wholesale shop in Kano. Her TPS records each sale. Her MIS shows best-selling lines weekly.

Before buying stock, she uses a DSS to compare expected demand and cash. Her EIS shows monthly profit. If she adopts ERP, the same sale updates stock and accounts. This shows the chain from routine data to decisions.

keyPoints: Transaction processing systems record routine events and must be fast and reliable.
Management information systems turn transaction data into regular reports for monitoring performance.
Decision support systems combine data with models to help with less routine choices.
Executive information systems give senior managers a concise view of key indicators.
ERP integrates shared modules and one database so one event can update several business functions.
E-commerce uses information systems for online trade and creates needs for security, delivery and returns handling.

en.title: Intermediate programming and scripting
en.short: Objects, modules, exceptions, files, APIs, testing and version control for intermediate programmers.

sections.heading: Objects and modules
sections.text: Object-oriented programming groups data and behaviour into classes. A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance. Encapsulation keeps state behind methods, inheritance lets a class reuse another, and polymorphism lets different classes answer the same call. A module is one reusable source file; a library is a collection of modules. Importing gives a namespace, so names do not clash. Package managers record dependencies in a manifest and lock file for repeatable installs.

sections.heading: Errors and files
sections.text: An exception is a runtime error signalled by the program or raised deliberately. In Python, a try block runs risky code, except handles named exceptions, else runs when no error occurs, and finally always runs for cleanup. Catch only what you can handle; swallowing errors hides bugs. File handling opens, reads or writes, then closes a file. A context manager such as with open(...) closes the file even after an error. State text encoding and use binary mode for non-text data.

sections.heading: APIs and testing
sections.text: An API is a defined interface that lets one piece of software use another, such as a library, an operating system or a web service. A web API usually exchanges HTTP requests and JSON responses; check status codes, validate fields, handle timeouts and rate limits, and never hard-code secrets. Testing checks behaviour against expected results. A unit test calls one small unit with fixed inputs and asserts the output; integration tests check modules or services together. Automated tests run on every change and catch regressions. Write tests for normal, boundary and error cases. Case: a campus results checker calls a results API, parses JSON, and tests a 404 response.

sections.heading: Version control
sections.text: Version control records changes so you can review, undo and collaborate. In Git, a commit is a snapshot, a branch is a movable line of work, and a merge combines branches. Conflicts happen when both sides change the same lines; resolve them by editing and testing. Commit small changes often, pull before pushing, and never commit passwords or generated files.

keyPoints: A class defines state and behaviour; an object is an instance of that class.
Encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism are the main object-oriented ideas.
Modules and libraries allow code reuse, and package managers make installs repeatable.
Handle only exceptions you can recover from, and use finally or context managers for cleanup.
Test units and integrations automatically, including boundary and error cases, and check API status codes.
Use version control with small commits, branches and merges, and never commit secrets.

en.title: Database design and normalisation
en.short: ER modelling, relational keys, integrity constraints, functional dependencies and normal forms to BCNF.

sections.heading: Entity relationship modelling
sections.text:
An entity relationship (ER) model describes data as entities, attributes and relationships. An entity is a thing about which data is kept, such as Student. An attribute is a property, such as student number. A relationship links entities, for example Enrols between Student and Course.

Cardinality states how many instances may take part: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. A key attribute identifies each entity instance. ER modelling is done before tables are built so users and designers agree the data meaning.

sections.heading: Relational model and keys
sections.text:
The relational model stores data in relations: tables with rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row; one is chosen as the primary key.

A foreign key is an attribute in one relation that refers to another relation’s primary key. For example, Enrolment(student_id, course_id, grade) has composite primary key (student_id, course_id), and each part is a foreign key to Student and Course.

sections.heading: Integrity constraints
sections.text:
Integrity constraints are rules the database must always satisfy. Entity integrity says a primary key cannot be null. Referential integrity says a foreign key must match an existing primary key value or be null if allowed.

Domain integrity restricts values to a valid type or range. A database management system can enforce these rules, protecting consistency.

sections.heading: Dependencies and normal forms
sections.text:
A functional dependency (FD) X → Y means each X value determines one Y value. Normalisation reduces redundancy and anomalies by decomposing relations. First normal form (1NF) requires atomic values. Second normal form (2NF) removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key. Third normal form (3NF) removes transitive dependencies: every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key. BCNF is stricter: for every non-trivial FD X → Y, X must be a superkey.

Example: Enrolment(student_id, course_id, student_name, grade) has student_id → student_name. This violates 2NF: student_name depends on part of the key, a partial dependency. Split into Student(student_id, student_name) and Enrolment(student_id, course_id, grade). Both are in 3NF and BCNF.

keyPoints: An ER model captures entities, attributes, relationships and cardinality before tables are designed.
A candidate key is minimal and unique; the chosen one is the primary key, and foreign keys refer to primary keys.
Entity integrity forbids null primary keys; referential integrity requires valid foreign key matches.
A functional dependency X → Y means X determines Y.
1NF needs atomic values; 2NF removes partial dependencies; 3NF removes transitive dependencies.
BCNF requires every non-trivial determinant to be a superkey.

en.title: SQL and database administration
en.short: SQL DDL and DML, joins, subqueries, views, transactions, indexes, privileges, backup and recovery.

sections.heading: DDL and DML
Joins and subqueries
sections.text:
Joins combine rows from tables using a condition. An inner join returns matching rows; left, right and full outer joins also keep unmatched rows. Example: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id; lists customers who have orders.

A subquery is a SELECT inside another statement. It can return one value, a list for IN, or be tested with EXISTS. A correlated subquery refers to the outer query and may run once per outer row.

sections.heading: Views and transactions
sections.text:
A view is a stored query used like a table. It can hide columns, simplify joins and restrict rows, but it is not always updatable.

A transaction groups statements into one unit of work. ACID means atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. COMMIT saves the work; ROLLBACK undoes it; SAVEPOINT marks a partial rollback point. Isolation levels vary by DBMS.

sections.heading: Indexes, privileges, backup
sections.text:
An index is a separate structure, often a B-tree, that speeds lookups. It uses storage and slows INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, so index columns used in WHERE and JOIN conditions, not every column.

Privileges control who may read or change data. GRANT gives privileges such as SELECT; REVOKE removes them. Roles group privileges. Follow least privilege: give each user only what the job needs. A full backup copies everything; an incremental backup copies changes since the last backup. Recovery restores the backup and applies transaction logs to a consistent point. Test restores regularly, because exact commands and recovery options depend on the DBMS.

keyPoints: DDL defines schema objects; DML reads and changes rows.
Inner joins return matching rows; outer joins keep unmatched rows.
A subquery is a SELECT inside another statement, and a correlated subquery can run once per outer row.
A view is a stored query, and a transaction is a unit of work that COMMIT or ROLLBACK ends.
Indexes speed lookups but use storage and slow writes.
Use GRANT and REVOKE with least privilege, and test backup recovery.

en.title: Web development: accessible and secure pages
en.short: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, responsive layout, forms, server-side scripting, accessibility and web security.

sections.heading: Markup and style
sections.text: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the structure and meaning of a page with elements such as headings, paragraphs, lists and links. Use the element that matches the content, not one chosen for its look. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls presentation: colour, spacing, type and layout. Keep style in CSS rather than in HTML attributes so the page is easier to maintain.

sections.heading: Behaviour and layout
sections.text: JavaScript is the scripting language that runs in the browser. It can respond to clicks, update the page and check input before it is sent. Responsive layout makes one page work on phones, tablets and desktops. It uses fluid grids, flexible images and CSS media queries, which apply different rules at different viewport widths. Test at several widths rather than assuming one breakpoint fits all.

sections.heading: Forms and server side
sections.text: Forms collect data with input, select and textarea elements. Every field needs a label, and the label should be tied to the field so screen readers announce it. Browser validation gives quick feedback but is not a security control. Server-side scripting runs on the web server, often in PHP, Python, Node.js or Java. It receives the request, validates every value again, talks to a database and returns HTML or JSON.

sections.heading: Accessibility and security
sections.text: Accessibility means people with disabilities can use the site. Use semantic HTML, text alternatives for images, enough colour contrast, visible focus and full keyboard operation. The W3C’s Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) give the accepted criteria. Basic web security follows from distrusting input. Escape output to reduce cross-site scripting (XSS), use parameterised queries against SQL injection, serve pages over HTTPS and store passwords with a slow password-hashing function. Case: a login form checks for empty fields in JavaScript, but the server repeats the check and hashes the password; if it trusted the browser, an attacker could post directly to it.

keyPoints: HTML gives structure and meaning; CSS controls presentation.
JavaScript adds behaviour in the browser, but the server must validate again.
Responsive layout uses fluid grids, flexible images and media queries.
Every form field needs a label, and labels must be tied to their fields.
Accessibility covers semantic HTML, keyboard use, contrast and text alternatives.
Basic web security: escape output, use parameterised queries, HTTPS and slow password hashing.

en.title: Systems analysis and design
en.short: The SDLC, requirements gathering, process and data models, UML, agile methods and documentation.

sections.heading: The life cycle
sections.text:
A systems development life cycle (SDLC) is the set of stages a team moves through to build an information system: planning and feasibility, analysis, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance.

In the waterfall model the stages run in order, each ending with a sign-off document before the next begins. This gives control and a clear record, but a mistake found late is expensive, because finished work must be redone.

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.text:
Requirements gathering (elicitation) finds what the system must do. Analysts interview users, run workshops, send questionnaires, watch work as it happens, read existing forms and reports, and show prototypes.

Requirements are functional (what the system does) or non-functional (quality: speed, security, usability). Each is written so it can be tested, then checked with users. Case: a clinic booking system in Kano must work on a slow connection. That is non-functional, and it shapes the design.

sections.heading: Modelling and UML
sections.text:
Process models describe what the system does and how data moves through it. Data flow diagrams (a context diagram, then levelled diagrams) show processes, data stores, external entities and flows. Data models show what is stored: entity relationship diagrams (ERDs) give entities, attributes, relationships and cardinality, such as one-to-many.

UML is a standard notation: use case diagrams for actors and goals, class diagrams for structure, sequence diagrams for message order over time, and activity diagrams for workflow.

sections.heading: Agile and documentation
sections.text:
Agile approaches deliver in short iterations, valuing working software and user feedback over heavy up-front documents. Scrum uses a product backlog of user stories, fixed-length sprints, a daily stand-up and a review at the end of each sprint.

Documentation still matters: user stories, test cases, architecture notes, a data dictionary and a user manual. Safety-critical or government systems often still need formal specifications, so fit the approach to the risk.

keyPoints: The SDLC runs from feasibility and analysis through design, build, test, deployment and maintenance.
Waterfall is sequential and document-driven; late changes are costly.
Functional requirements state what the system does; non-functional ones state qualities such as speed and security.
Data flow diagrams model processes and flows; ERDs model stored data and cardinality.
UML use case, class, sequence and activity diagrams describe different views of a system.
Agile delivers in iterations with user feedback, but documentation such as test cases and user guides still matters.

en.title: Data communications and networks
en.short: OSI and TCP/IP layers, IPv4 subnetting, routing, switching, wireless LANs and common protocols.

sections.heading: Layered models
sections.text: The OSI reference model has seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. It is a teaching model. The TCP/IP model has four layers: network access, internet, transport and application. Each layer provides a service to the layer above and adds a header, a process called encapsulation. Routers mainly work at the network layer and switches at the data link layer.

sections.heading: IP addressing
sections.text:
An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers. A prefix length, such as /26, gives the subnet mask. The network part identifies the subnet; the host part identifies the device. CIDR allows any prefix length. IPv6 uses 128 bits. Private addresses are not routed on the public Internet; check current ranges.

Example: 192.168.10.0/26. The mask is 255.255.255.192. The block size is 256 − 192 = 64. Subnets start at .0, .64, .128 and .192. For .0/26, usable hosts are .1 to .62, broadcast is .63, and there are 2^6 − 2 = 62 hosts.

sections.heading: Routing and switching
sections.text: A switch learns MAC addresses and forwards frames only to the port where the destination is known. VLANs divide one physical switch into separate broadcast domains. A router forwards packets between networks using a routing table. Longest prefix match wins. Static routes are set by hand; dynamic protocols such as OSPF and BGP exchange routes automatically. RIP is an older distance-vector protocol. A default route is used when no other route matches.

sections.heading: Wireless and protocols
sections.text: A wireless LAN uses radio waves under the IEEE 802.11 family. A station joins a wireless network through an access point; the network name is the SSID. Because stations cannot reliably detect collisions, 802.11 uses CSMA/CA with acknowledgements. Common Internet protocols include DNS for name resolution, DHCP for automatic address configuration, HTTP and HTTPS for the web, SMTP for mail transfer, TCP for reliable streams and UDP for low-overhead datagrams. TLS secures many protocols. Port numbers identify services on a host.

keyPoints: OSI has seven layers; TCP/IP has four, and encapsulation adds headers at each layer.
An IPv4 address is 32 bits and a prefix length defines the network and host parts.
For a /26 subnet the mask is 255.255.255.192, block size is 64, and usable hosts are 2^6 − 2 = 62.
Routers forward by longest prefix match; switches forward frames using MAC address tables.
IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs use CSMA/CA, and common protocols include DNS, DHCP, HTTP, TCP and UDP.

en.title: Network administration
en.short: Configuring routers and switches, VLANs, DHCP, DNS, monitoring, troubleshooting and network policies.

sections.heading: Devices and VLANs
sections.text:
A router forwards packets between IP networks. A switch forwards frames inside a local network. Configuration sets management addresses, hostname, passwords, interfaces, default gateway and routing.

On switches, access ports carry one VLAN and trunk ports carry several using tags (IEEE 802.1Q). A VLAN is a broadcast domain, so different VLANs need a router or Layer 3 switch to communicate. Example: in a Lagos campus, staff ports in VLAN 10 and student ports in VLAN 20 share one switch but do not broadcast to each other.

sections.heading: Addressing services
sections.text:
DHCP gives hosts an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS server for a lease period. A DHCP relay forwards requests across subnets. Reservations keep a fixed address for a server or printer.

DNS maps names to addresses and stores records such as A for IPv4, AAAA for IPv6, CNAME for an alias and MX for mail. Administrators create zones and set forwarders. Example: a DHCP scope 192.168.10.0/24 might hand out .100 to .200 and reserve .10 for the printer.

sections.heading: Monitoring and troubleshooting
sections.text:
Monitoring collects interface status, traffic, errors, CPU and logs. SNMP polls devices, and syslog sends logs to a central server. Baselines show normal behaviour, so alerts are meaningful.

Troubleshooting works layer by layer: check cable and link lights, then IP address and gateway, then DNS, then routing and firewall rules. Commands such as ping, traceroute and device show commands give evidence. Change control records each change so faults can be reversed.

sections.heading: Policies and practice
sections.text:
Network policies state who may connect, what they may access, how passwords and devices are managed, and how changes and backups are handled. An acceptable use policy, access control lists, configuration backups and documentation are controls.

Policies should be reviewed and enforced, not just written. In a small organisation one administrator may do all these tasks; in a large one they are split between network, security and service teams.

keyPoints: Routers forward packets between IP networks; switches forward frames inside a local network.
Access ports carry one VLAN and trunk ports carry several VLANs with tags such as IEEE 802.1Q.
DHCP supplies addresses and options for a lease, and DNS resolves names to addresses.
Monitoring needs baselines, logs and interface errors so alerts are meaningful.
Troubleshoot from the physical layer upward using ping, traceroute and device show commands.
Network policies cover acceptable use, access control, change management and backups.

en.title: Information security and risk management
en.short: CIA goals, threats and controls, risk assessment with ALE, cryptography, access control and incident response.

sections.heading: CIA triad and threats
sections.text:
Information security protects information in storage, transmission or use. Its three goals are confidentiality, integrity and availability, called the CIA triad. Confidentiality means only authorised people can read data. Integrity means data is accurate and cannot be changed without detection. Availability means authorised users can reach data when needed.

A threat is anything that could cause harm, such as malware, phishing, theft or fire. A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can exploit. A risk is the chance and impact of harm. Controls reduce risk and may be preventive, detective or corrective.

sections.heading: Controls and risk assessment
sections.text:
Risk assessment identifies assets, threats and vulnerabilities, then estimates likelihood and impact. A quantitative method uses single loss expectancy (SLE), the cost of one incident, and annualised rate of occurrence (ARO), the expected incidents per year. Annualised loss expectancy (ALE) = SLE × ARO. Example: an outage costs 400,000 naira per event and is expected twice a year, so ALE = 400,000 × 2 = 800,000 naira. A control is worth implementing if its annual cost is less than the reduction in ALE it achieves.

Controls include policies, training, encryption, backups, firewalls and locks. Access control applies least privilege: give each user only the access needed. Authentication proves identity; authorisation decides what that identity may do. Role-based access control grants rights by job role.

sections.heading: Cryptography and access
sections.text: Cryptography protects confidentiality and integrity. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for encryption and decryption and is fast, but key distribution is hard. Asymmetric encryption uses a public key and a private key. It helps with key exchange and digital signatures, which prove origin and integrity. A hash function turns data into a fixed-length digest; it is one way and changes completely if the data changes. Do not invent ciphers; manage keys carefully.

sections.heading: Incident response
sections.text: Incident response is the planned handling of a security event. Common phases are preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and lessons learned. Containment stops spread, eradication removes the cause, and recovery restores safe service. Record actions and review.

keyPoints: Confidentiality, integrity and availability are the three goals of information security.
A threat exploits a vulnerability, and a control reduces the resulting risk.
Risk assessment estimates likelihood and impact; ALE = SLE × ARO.
Symmetric encryption uses one shared key; asymmetric encryption uses a public and private key pair, and hashing checks integrity.
Authentication proves identity, authorisation grants permissions, and least privilege limits access.
Incident response follows preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned.

en.title: Cloud computing and virtualisation
en.short: Cloud service and deployment models, virtual machines and containers, storage, elasticity and SLAs.

sections.heading: Service models
sections.text: Cloud computing is on-demand delivery of computing resources over a network, paid for by use. In IaaS (infrastructure as a service) the provider supplies virtual machines, storage and networks, and the customer manages the operating system upward. In PaaS (platform as a service) the provider also manages the runtime and databases, so developers deploy code without tending servers. In SaaS (software as a service) the customer simply uses a finished application such as webmail. The more the provider manages, the less control the customer keeps.

sections.heading: Deployment models
sections.text: A public cloud is shared infrastructure owned by a provider. A private cloud serves one organisation, on its own premises or a provider’s. A community cloud is shared by organisations with common requirements, such as several universities. A hybrid cloud joins two or more of these and moves workloads between them.

sections.heading: Machines and containers
sections.text:
A virtual machine (VM) is a complete guest operating system running on a hypervisor, software that divides the physical CPU, memory and disk among guests. A type 1 hypervisor runs on bare hardware; a type 2 runs on a host operating system. Containers share the host kernel and package only the application and its libraries, so they start in seconds and are lighter, but isolate less strongly.

Example: a host with 64 GB of RAM and 16 cores. If each VM needs 8 GB and 2 cores, at most 8 VMs fit. Containers of 512 MB would number far more by memory alone, though they share the same cores.

sections.heading: Storage, elasticity, SLAs
sections.text: Object storage keeps files as objects with metadata in buckets, which are named storage areas; block storage provides virtual disks; file storage provides shared directories. Elasticity is automatic growth and shrinkage of resources with demand; scalability is the capacity to grow at all. Live migration moves a running VM to another host with little downtime. A service level agreement (SLA) sets measurable commitments, usually availability, and the remedy if they are missed. Availability of 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month (43,200 × 0.001).

keyPoints: IaaS supplies virtual infrastructure, PaaS a managed platform, SaaS a finished application.
Public, private, community and hybrid are the main deployment models.
A VM runs its own operating system on a hypervisor; a container shares the host kernel and is lighter.
Object, block and file are the three common cloud storage types.
Elasticity adds and removes resources automatically; migration moves workloads between hosts.
An SLA states measurable service commitments and the remedy for missing them.

en.title: Data analytics and business intelligence
en.short: Data warehouses, ETL, OLAP, reporting, dashboards, visualisation, basic statistics and data quality.

sections.heading: Warehouse and ETL
sections.text: A data warehouse is a central store built for analysis, not daily transactions. It is subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile: data is organised by subject, cleaned to common definitions, kept with history and stable once loaded. ETL means extract, transform, load. Extract copies data from sources. Transform cleans, deduplicates and conforms it to shared definitions. Load writes it into the warehouse through staging tables, temporary tables that hold data during the load. A retailer in Kano with two shops may load daily sales into one warehouse so managers compare shops on the same product codes.

sections.heading: OLAP and reporting
sections.text: Business intelligence (BI) turns data into decisions. OLAP, online analytical processing, lets users view data as a multidimensional cube: dimensions such as product, month and branch, and measures such as sales and profit. Operations include roll-up (summarise to a higher level), drill-down (go to detail), slice and dice (filter subsets) and pivot (rotate axes). Reporting presents regular, structured results, such as a monthly sales report. A dashboard shows key performance indicators (KPIs) at a glance, often with charts and filters. Reports answer defined questions; dashboards monitor current performance.

sections.heading: Visualisation and statistics
sections.text: Visualisation turns numbers into charts. Use bars for categories, lines for trends over time and scatter plots for relationships. Start axes at zero for bar charts and label units, because a cut axis can mislead. Basic statistics summarise data. For daily sales 20, 22, 24, 26 and 28: mean = 120 ÷ 5 = 24. Population variance = [(−4)² + (−2)² + 0² + 2² + 4²] ÷ 5 = 40 ÷ 5 = 8, so standard deviation = √8 ≈ 2.83. The median is 24. Correlation measures linear association, not cause.

sections.heading: Data quality
sections.text: Data quality means fitness for use. Common dimensions are accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness and validity. Poor quality often comes from duplicate records, missing fields, inconsistent codes and late loading. Controls include validation at entry, source reconciliation, duplicate checks, clear data definitions and stewardship. Quality must be measured and reported, not assumed.

keyPoints: Business intelligence turns data into decisions using warehouses, ETL, OLAP, reports and dashboards.
A data warehouse holds integrated, historical, non-volatile data for analysis, not daily transactions.
ETL extracts, transforms and loads data; transformation does most of the cleaning and conforming.
OLAP supports roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice and pivot on multidimensional cubes.
For n values, mean = Σx ÷ n and population variance = Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n; standard deviation = √variance.
Data quality is judged on accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness and validity.

en.title: Human-computer interaction
en.short: Usability principles, user-centred design, prototyping, evaluation methods and inclusive design.

sections.heading: Usability principles
sections.text:
Usability is the extent to which specified users can reach specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a given context of use (ISO 9241-11). Effectiveness is doing the task correctly, efficiency is the effort it costs, satisfaction is how the user feels.

Principles help: show system status, use the user’s own words, stay consistent, prevent errors, allow undo, and prefer recognition over recall. Jakob Nielsen’s ten heuristics are a common checklist.

sections.heading: User-centred design
sections.text:
User-centred design involves real users instead of guessing at their needs. ISO 9241-210 describes four repeating activities: understand the context of use, specify user requirements, produce design solutions, and evaluate them against those requirements. Users take part in each round.

Designers are not typical users. They know the system too well to see what confuses a first-time user.

sections.heading: Prototyping
sections.text:
A prototype is an early model of the interface. Low-fidelity prototypes, such as paper sketches, are cheap and draw honest criticism because nobody mistakes them for a finished product. High-fidelity prototypes behave like the real system; they test detail well but cost more.

Case: Amina’s team is building a course-registration portal at a college in Ibadan. They sketch the screens, test them with six students, find that the fee-status page confuses everyone, and fix it before writing code.

sections.heading: Evaluation and accessibility
sections.text:
Evaluation is formative when it runs during design to find problems, summative when it judges the finished product against targets. Usability testing watches representative users attempt real tasks and notes where they fail. Heuristic evaluation has experts check the interface against principles; questionnaires such as the System Usability Scale give a comparable score.

Accessibility means people with disabilities can use the product. The W3C’s Web Content Accessibility Guidelines rest on four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust. Level AA asks a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text. Inclusive design aims at the widest range of users from the start.

keyPoints: Usability means effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction for specified users and goals (ISO 9241-11).
User-centred design is iterative and involves users in every round (ISO 9241-210).
Low-fidelity prototypes are cheap and invite honest feedback; high-fidelity ones test detailed interaction.
Usability testing with real users on real tasks is the main way to find interface problems.
WCAG’s four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable and robust; level AA needs 4.5:1 contrast for normal text.
Accessibility and inclusive design consider disabled and excluded users from the start, not as a later fix.

en.title: Mobile application development
en.short: Mobile platforms, UI patterns, local storage, APIs, sensors, testing and app store release.

sections.heading: Platforms and UI
sections.text: Android and iOS are the two main mobile platforms. A native app is written in the platform’s own language and tools, such as Kotlin with Android Studio or Swift with Xcode. A cross-platform app shares much of its code, often using Flutter or React Native, but still needs platform testing. Mobile UI patterns suit small screens: a bottom tab bar for main areas, a list that opens a detail screen, clear forms, and visible back navigation. Ask for a permission only when a feature needs it, and explain why.

sections.heading: Data, APIs and sensors
sections.text:
Local storage keeps data on the phone. Key-value stores hold small settings; SQLite databases hold structured records; files hold images or documents. Sensitive values such as tokens belong in the platform’s secure storage, not plain files. An API (application programming interface) lets the app request data from a server, commonly over HTTPS using REST and JSON. Design for weak networks: cache responses, show loading and error states, and sync when online. Sensors include GPS, accelerometer, camera and microphone. They drain battery and need permission, so sample only when necessary.

Case: Ada builds a campus bus app in Lagos. It stores the timetable in SQLite, fetches live positions from an HTTPS API, and uses GPS only while the bus screen is open.

sections.heading: Testing and release
sections.text: Test at three levels: unit tests for logic, UI tests for screens, and manual tests on real devices with different screen sizes and network conditions. Emulators help but do not replace a physical phone. Before release, sign the app with a private key, set a version number, and prepare a privacy policy and store listing. Google Play and the Apple App Store review apps against their own rules, which change, so check the current official guidelines. Release to a small group first, watch crash reports, then expand.

keyPoints: Native apps use each platform’s own tools; cross-platform apps share code but still need device testing.
Use mobile UI patterns such as tab bars, list-detail screens and just-in-time permission requests.
Store small settings in key-value storage, structured data in SQLite, and secrets in secure storage.
Call server APIs over HTTPS, handle offline and error states, and cache data for weak networks.
Sensors such as GPS and the camera need permission and should run only when needed to save battery.
Test on real devices and follow the current Google Play or Apple App Store rules before release.

en.title: IT project management
en.short: Covers project life cycle, scope, schedule, cost, risk, quality, stakeholder communication, agile methods and tools.

sections.heading: Life cycle and scope
sections.text: A project is a temporary effort to create a unique product, service or result. Its life cycle normally runs through initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and control, and closure. Initiation defines the business case and the project charter, which authorises the work. Planning produces a scope statement: the deliverables, boundaries and acceptance criteria. Scope must be controlled, because unapproved additions cause scope creep, extra cost and delay. A work breakdown structure (WBS) divides scope into manageable packages.

sections.heading: Schedule and cost
sections.text: Scheduling orders WBS tasks, estimates durations and sets dependencies. The critical path is the longest dependent sequence; it sets the shortest possible duration, and any delay on it delays the project. Cost management estimates, budgets and controls spending. Earned value management compares planned value (PV), earned value (EV) and actual cost (AC). Example: PV=40,000, EV=30,000, AC=35,000. Cost variance (CV)=EV−AC=−5,000, so over budget. Schedule variance (SV)=EV−PV=−10,000, so behind schedule. Cost performance index (CPI)=EV÷AC=30,000÷35,000=0.857; schedule performance index (SPI)=EV÷PV=30,000÷40,000=0.75.

sections.heading: Risk, quality, people
sections.text: Risk is an uncertain event that may affect objectives. Teams record risks in a register, rate probability and impact, and plan responses: avoid, reduce, transfer or accept. Quality means meeting agreed requirements and fitness for purpose; acceptance criteria and testing make it measurable. Stakeholder communication identifies everyone affected, their information needs and the channels and frequency of updates. A simple communication plan prevents surprises.

sections.heading: Agile and tools
sections.text: Agile methods deliver work in short iterations, often called sprints. A product backlog lists requirements, daily stand-ups coordinate the team, and retrospectives improve the process. Agile suits changing requirements but still needs scope and cost control. Tools include Gantt charts for schedules, Kanban boards for workflow, issue trackers and collaboration software. Choice depends on the organisation; check local practice.

keyPoints: A project life cycle runs from initiation and planning through execution, monitoring and control to closure.
Scope defines deliverables and boundaries, and uncontrolled changes cause scope creep.
The critical path is the longest dependent sequence and sets the shortest project duration.
Cost variance CV=EV−AC and schedule variance SV=EV−PV; negative values mean over budget or behind schedule.
Cost performance index CPI=EV÷AC and schedule performance index SPI=EV÷PV; values below 1 are unfavourable.
Risk, quality and stakeholder communication are planned throughout, while agile methods use short iterations and tools such as Gantt charts and Kanban boards.

en.title: IT service management
en.short: Service life cycle, incident, problem and change management, SLAs, configuration management and ITIL.

sections.heading: Service life cycle
sections.text: A service delivers value to customers without the customer owning specific costs and risks. Service management is the set of capabilities for planning, delivering, supporting and improving services. ITIL v3 has five life-cycle stages: service strategy, design, transition, operation and continual service improvement. ITIL 4 replaces these stages with a service value chain and practices, but the life-cycle idea remains: a service is designed, built, run, reviewed and retired.

sections.heading: Incidents and problems
sections.text: An incident is an unplanned interruption to a service or a reduction in its quality. Incident management restores normal service quickly; it does not have to find the root cause. A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents. Problem management finds that cause and drives a permanent fix; a known error is a problem with a documented cause and workaround. Case: at a Lagos payroll office, Amina cannot log in. The service desk resets her password. When many staff report lockouts, it becomes a problem; the team traces it to a failed directory sync and schedules a fix.

sections.heading: Changes and configuration
sections.text: A change is an addition, modification or removal of anything that could affect services. Change management assesses risk, authorises work, schedules it and reviews the result. A change advisory board (CAB) advises on risky changes. Configuration management records configuration items (CIs), such as servers and applications, and their relationships in a configuration management database (CMDB). The CMDB supports impact analysis: before the directory fix, staff can see which payroll and email services depend on the directory server.

sections.heading: SLAs and frameworks
sections.text: A service level agreement (SLA) is an agreement between a provider and a customer. It states services, targets, responsibilities and remedies. An operational level agreement (OLA) supports an SLA between internal teams; an underpinning contract (UC) does the same with an external supplier. ITIL is a framework of best practice for service management. ISO/IEC 20000 is the international standard for service management systems, and COBIT is a governance framework. Frameworks guide practice; they do not replace judgement.

keyPoints: A service delivers value without the customer owning specific costs and risks.
Incident management restores service; problem management removes the underlying cause.
A known error is a problem with a documented cause and workaround.
Change management authorises and reviews changes; configuration management tracks CIs and their relationships in a CMDB.
An SLA is a customer agreement; an OLA is internal and a UC is with a supplier.
ITIL is a best-practice framework; ISO/IEC 20000 is a standard and COBIT is a governance framework.

en.title: Enterprise systems and e-business
en.short: ERP, CRM and supply chain systems, e-commerce models, integration and process change.

sections.heading: Enterprise systems
sections.text:
An enterprise system is software that supports processes across a whole organisation on one shared database. The main example is enterprise resource planning (ERP): modules for finance, procurement, inventory, production and human resources that post to the same records, so a dispatch note and an invoice cannot disagree.

ERP is bought as a package (SAP, Oracle and Microsoft Dynamics are common vendors) and carries built-in assumptions about how processes should run. Costs and failure rates vary widely.

sections.heading: Customers and supply
sections.text:
Customer relationship management (CRM) systems store customer details, contacts, quotations, sales pipeline and service tickets so that sales, support and accounts see one history. Analytical CRM reports on segments and churn; operational CRM runs the daily interactions.

Supply chain systems plan and track sourcing, production, stock and delivery, and share demand and stock data with suppliers. Poor sharing causes the bullwhip effect: small changes in retail demand become large swings in orders upstream.

sections.heading: E-commerce models
sections.text:
E-business covers all electronically enabled business processes; e-commerce is the narrower buying and selling part. Common models are business to business (B2B), business to consumer (B2C), consumer to consumer (C2C, as on marketplace platforms) and business to government (B2G).

Revenue can come from transactions, subscriptions or advertising. Payment, tax, delivery and consumer-protection rules differ by country, so check local law.

sections.heading: Integration and change
sections.text:
Integration joins systems so data flows without re-keying. Options include point-to-point links, middleware, an enterprise service bus or APIs; master data management keeps shared reference data (customer, product, supplier) consistent. Integration usually forces process change, and ERP projects often use business process reengineering: redesigning a process from the outcome rather than automating the old one.

Case: Adaeze Nwosu, finance manager at a Lagos distributor, cut order-to-cash from 12 days to 4 by invoicing at dispatch. At 600 orders a month and an average invoice of ₦180,000, receivables fall from 600 × 180,000 × 12/30 = ₦43.2m to 600 × 180,000 × 4/30 = ₦14.4m, releasing ₦28.8m (illustrative figures).

keyPoints: An ERP system runs many business processes on one shared database, so records agree across departments.
CRM supports sales, service and analysis of customer relationships, while supply chain systems share demand and stock data with suppliers.
The bullwhip effect is the amplification of small demand changes into large order swings upstream.
E-business is wider than e-commerce; B2B, B2C, C2C and B2G describe who trades with whom.
Integration uses point-to-point links, middleware, service buses or APIs, with master data management for shared reference data.
ERP and integration projects usually need business process reengineering, not just automation of existing steps.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and law
en.short: Codes of ethics, ethical theories, privacy and data protection, IP, cybercrime law and professional duty.

sections.heading: Codes and ethical theory
sections.text:
Professional codes state duties: competence, honesty, confidentiality and putting public safety first. Examples are the ACM Code of Ethics, the BCS Code of Conduct and the IEEE Code of Ethics. They guide judgement but are not law.

Ethical theories give reasons for a decision. Utilitarianism judges an act by its consequences for everyone affected. Deontology judges it by duties and rules, whatever the outcome. Virtue ethics asks what a person of good character would do.

Case: a developer finds a security flaw in a hospital system. A utilitarian weighs the harm avoided by disclosure; a deontologist may hold that the duty to warn patients is unconditional.

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection
sections.text:
Privacy is a person’s control over information about themselves. Data protection law sets rules for handling personal data: a lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimisation, security, and rights of access and erasure.

Examples: the EU GDPR (Regulation 2016/679, applied from 2018); Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023; South Africa’s POPIA (Act 4 of 2013, in force 2021); Kenya’s Data Protection Act 2019. Rules and penalties differ, so check the current national law.

sections.heading: Intellectual property
sections.text:
Copyright protects expression, not ideas, and arises automatically. Patents protect inventions and need registration; under the TRIPS agreement a patent lasts at least 20 years from filing. Trademarks protect signs of origin. Trade secrets protect confidential information.

Terms vary: copyright commonly lasts the author’s life plus 70 years, but this differs by country and by type of work. Nigeria’s Copyright Act 2022 is one national example.

sections.heading: Cybercrime and responsibility
sections.text:
Cybercrime laws create offences such as unauthorised access and unauthorised interference with data. Computer fraud is also a crime, but the law that covers it differs by country. Examples: the UK Computer Misuse Act 1990, Nigeria’s Cybercrimes Act 2015 and South Africa’s Cybercrimes Act 19 of 2020.
