Professional responsibility means working within your competence, keeping records, reporting risks, and refusing work you cannot do safely. Whistleblowing, reporting wrongdoing, is a last resort after internal channels fail.

keyPoints: Professional codes set duties but do not replace the law.
Utilitarianism looks at consequences; deontology looks at duties; virtue ethics looks at character.
Data protection law requires a lawful basis, limited purpose and security for personal data.
Copyright is automatic; patents and trademarks need registration.
Cybercrime laws in the UK, Nigeria and South Africa punish unauthorised access; computer fraud is also a crime.
Professional responsibility includes competence, record keeping, reporting risk and whistleblowing.

en.title: Advanced data management and big data
en.short: Distributed databases, NoSQL models, data lakes, big data architectures, consistency trade-offs and governance.

sections.heading: Distributed databases
sections.text: A distributed database stores data on several nodes but is queried as one logical database. Replication keeps copies for availability and read speed; sharding splits rows or documents across nodes so each node holds a subset. The hard part is coordination: a transaction may touch several nodes, and the system must decide how to commit it and what to do when a node or network link fails.

sections.heading: NoSQL and data lakes
sections.text: NoSQL models trade some relational guarantees for flexible schemas and scale. Key-value stores map keys to values; document stores hold JSON-like documents; wide-column stores organise rows into column families; graph stores hold nodes and edges for relationship queries. A data lake stores raw files in native formats and applies schema on read, meaning structure is imposed when data is read, not when written. A warehouse usually applies schema on write. Without catalogues and controls, a lake can become a data swamp.

sections.heading: Big data architectures
sections.text: Big data architectures combine storage, processing and orchestration. Batch processing handles bounded historical data; stream processing handles continuous events with low delay. The lambda architecture runs a batch layer and a speed layer, while the kappa architecture treats all data as a stream. Partitioning, parallel processing and distributed file systems let work spread across many machines.

sections.heading: Consistency, scalability and governance
sections.text: Scalability is vertical (a bigger machine) or horizontal (more machines). Horizontal scale brings the CAP trade-off: during a network partition a system cannot guarantee both strong consistency and availability. Eventual consistency allows temporary stale reads. PACELC adds that even without partitions, consistency costs latency. Data governance sets ownership, quality rules, access control, lineage, retention and privacy. A Lagos retailer, for example, streams sales events to a lake, but Ngozi, the data steward, must document each dataset and restrict customer data under local law.

keyPoints: Replication improves availability and read speed; sharding spreads data across nodes.
NoSQL models include key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores.
A data lake uses schema on read; a warehouse usually uses schema on write.
Batch processing handles bounded data; stream processing handles continuous events.
CAP says a partitioned system cannot guarantee both strong consistency and availability.
Data governance covers ownership, quality, access, lineage, retention and privacy, and must follow the law of each country.

en.title: Cybersecurity governance and digital forensics
en.short: Security governance, risk and compliance, incident response, forensic process and evidence law.

sections.heading: Governance and risk
sections.text:
Security governance sets direction: who decides, who is accountable, and how controls are measured. Frameworks such as ISO/IEC 27001 for an information security management system, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, and COBIT give structure. They align security with law and business aims.

Risk management identifies assets, threats and vulnerabilities, estimates likelihood and impact, then treats risk by avoiding, reducing, transferring or accepting it. Compliance means meeting duties from regulators, contracts and standards. Evidence includes policies, risk registers and audit logs.

sections.heading: Incident response
sections.text:
Incident response is the organised reaction to a security event. A common lifecycle is preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and lessons learned. Preparation covers roles, playbooks and tested backups. Preserve logs before rebuilding systems.

Case: Ngozi, an IT officer at a Lagos college, finds malware on a staff laptop. The team isolates it, images the disk, records who handled it and when, and seals the original. They notify management and follow the applicable data protection law if personal data may be exposed.

sections.heading: Forensics and evidence
sections.text:
Digital forensics follows a repeatable process: identification, preservation, acquisition, examination, analysis and reporting. A write blocker prevents changes during imaging. A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 is calculated before and after copying; matching hashes support integrity.

Chain of custody records every transfer of evidence: who had it, when and why. Weak documentation can make evidence unreliable or inadmissible. Admissibility rules vary by country and case.

sections.heading: Legal and ethical issues
sections.text:
Forensic work needs lawful authority. Searching a person’s device without consent or a warrant may breach privacy and computer misuse laws; these differ by country. The EU GDPR and Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 are examples of data protection rules, not universal law.

Ethically, investigators should be competent, impartial and proportionate, minimise intrusion into private data, and report findings honestly, including weaknesses in their methods. The expert’s duty is to truth, not the client’s preferred outcome.

keyPoints: Governance assigns accountability and aligns security with law and business aims.
Risk is treated by avoiding, reducing, transferring or accepting it; compliance is evidence of meeting duties.
Incident response follows preparation, detection, containment, recovery and lessons learned.
Digital forensics follows identification, preservation, acquisition, examination, analysis and reporting.
Chain of custody and hash values support evidence integrity and admissibility.
Legal authority, privacy and impartiality are essential ethical duties.

en.title: Cloud-native architecture and edge computing
en.short: Microservices, containers, orchestration, serverless, edge and fog computing, latency, resilience and security.

sections.heading: From monolith to microservices
sections.text: A monolith is one deployable application. Microservices split it into small services, each built around a business capability and independently deployable. They communicate over network calls and usually own their data. This allows independent scaling and release, but adds network failure, versioning and data consistency problems. For example, a college portal can separate identity, results and fees; the results team can deploy without rebuilding fees.

sections.heading: Containers and orchestration
sections.text: A container packages an application with its dependencies and runs on a shared operating system core, so it is lighter than a virtual machine. An image is the built package; a registry stores images. An orchestrator schedules containers, restarts failed ones, scales them and connects services. Kubernetes is a common orchestrator. It works from a declared desired state, so operators describe what should run and the system reconciles reality.

sections.heading: Serverless and edge
sections.text: Serverless computing runs event-driven functions on managed infrastructure. The provider handles servers, scales automatically and bills per use; start-up delays and execution limits are trade-offs. Edge computing processes data near users or devices to reduce latency, the delay in a round trip. Fog computing adds an intermediate layer between edge and cloud for coordination and aggregation. Case: a Lagos traffic camera detects an incident locally and sends only a summary to the cloud; a fog node combines several cameras.

sections.heading: Resilience and security
sections.text: Resilience is the ability to keep serving during failure. Useful patterns are timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers that stop calls to a failing part, and redundant instances. Security must cover every service and device: encrypt traffic, authenticate both ends, give each part only the access it needs, protect secrets, verify image signatures and patch promptly. Edge devices are physically exposed, so key storage and updates need care. Data protection rules differ by country; check the current law.

keyPoints: Microservices are independently deployable services that own their data and communicate over network calls.
Containers share the host operating system core; orchestrators such as Kubernetes schedule and reconcile them.
Serverless functions scale automatically but face start-up delays and execution limits.
Edge computing cuts latency by processing near users; fog adds a coordination layer.
Resilience uses timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers and redundancy.
Secure cloud-native and edge systems with encryption, least access, secrets protection, image verification and patching.

en.title: Research methods in information technology
en.short: Research design, literature review, qualitative and quantitative methods, ethics and dissertation planning.

sections.heading: Design and review
sections.text: Research design is the plan that links a question to evidence. Exploratory, descriptive and explanatory designs answer different questions. A design may be fixed in advance (quantitative) or emergent (qualitative). The literature review is a critical synthesis of existing work, not a list of summaries. It shows the gap your study addresses and shapes the question, theory and method. In information technology, review both academic sources and credible industry reports, and record how you searched.

sections.heading: Methods and data
sections.text: Quantitative methods measure variables and test hypotheses with numbers; surveys and experiments are common. Qualitative methods explore meanings and experiences through interviews, observation or documents. Mixed methods combine both. Sampling is choosing participants or cases. Probability sampling supports statistical generalisation; purposive sampling selects information-rich cases. Data collection must be piloted and documented. Analysis for quantitative data uses descriptive statistics and then tests such as correlation or regression, checking assumptions. Qualitative analysis often uses coding, grouping text into themes. Reliability, validity and triangulation judge quality; triangulation means cross-checking findings with more than one method or source. Example: Ada studies mobile-money adoption among traders in Enugu. She surveys 200 traders and interviews 12, then compares survey patterns with interview themes.

sections.heading: Research ethics
sections.text: Research ethics protects people and data. Seek informed consent, explain purpose and risks, keep confidentiality, and allow withdrawal. An ethics committee must approve studies involving human participants. Handle personal data lawfully; data protection rules differ by country, so check the current national law and your institution’s policy. Avoid fabrication, falsification and plagiarism; cite sources and keep raw data securely.

sections.heading: Proposal and planning
sections.text: A research proposal states the problem, question, objectives, brief literature gap, design, methods, ethics and timetable. A dissertation plan turns this into milestones: proposal approval, ethics clearance, pilot, fieldwork, analysis, writing and revision. Keep a research journal and back up data. Agree supervision meetings and record decisions. Plan for delays in access or recruitment. The final dissertation reports methods honestly, including limitations, so readers can judge the claims.

keyPoints: Research design links a clear question to appropriate evidence.
A literature review synthesises sources and identifies the gap you will address.
Quantitative methods test hypotheses with numbers; qualitative methods explore meanings and experiences.
Sampling, piloting and documented collection affect data quality.
Ethics approval, informed consent and lawful data handling are required before collecting human data.
A proposal and milestone plan keep a dissertation focused, supervised and on schedule.
